title: W0299 `borrow_projection_copy` IS SILENT WHEN A BORROW PROJECTION IS PASSED TO A USER CALLEE THAT KEEPS IT -- `keep(w.r, mut v)`, a storing associated function and `k.put(w.r)` each copy the field and run its `Drop` body twice on every surface, and none of them warns; the lint fires only for the `Vec.push` builtin argument and a TRAIT associated-function argument. design.md now says which call copies (d618ccbcf), so the rule to implement is settled
detail:
SPLIT OUT of B-2026-09-14-10 at its close. That row's open question was whether the discard-elision should exist; Gowtham decided on 2026-09-26 to keep it, and d618ccbcf documents it in design.md § "Field projection off a borrow". What remains is the lint: it should warn exactly when the callee keeps the argument, and today it misses every user callee that does.

The measurement is B-2026-09-14-10's 2026-09-17 table (Group B, x86_64 Linux at f1cf626), with `karac check` per cell:

    cell                              copies?   warns?
    consume(w.r)   free, discards      no        no      correct
    v.push(w.r)    builtin, stores     YES       YES     correct
    keep(w.r,..)   free, stores        YES       no      MISSED
    Sk.take(w.r)   assoc, discards     no        no      correct
    k.put(w.r)     method, stores      YES       no      MISSED
    let m = w.r    let initializer     YES       YES     correct (control)

The same table also needs a storing ASSOCIATED function, which was not measured there.

WHY IT IS MISSED, from that note: the user-method-argument warning sits in `dispatch_trait_assoc_fn` (the trait associated-function path), which an inherent `impl K { fn put(mut ref self, x: R) }` call never reaches, and a free-function argument has no warning site at all. The blocker the row recorded is that the call site has the parameter TYPE but not the callee's AST `Function`, which `fn_moves_param_into_outliving_place` needs to answer "does the callee keep it". Codegen already answers that question to decide whether to copy, so the lint and the copy should ask the same predicate rather than two that can drift.
fix: 52ee6bb0ae (the v2 core's move rules as errors, C3), pinned by 0206d8dcd1. The row wanted W0299 to warn where a borrow projection went to a user callee that keeps it, because legacy copied the field and ran its Drop body twice. Under core-semantics §3.7 moving a non-`Copy` value out of a `ref`-rooted place is an error, so there is no silent copy left to warn about. Re-measured on the v2 pipeline at 1857b7091b, `karac check` and `__mir-run` per cell: `keep(w.r, mut v)` with `x: own D` (free, stores), `kk.put(w.r)` (inherent method, stores) and `K.make(w.r)` (associated function, stores) each fail with `error[borrow_projection_copy]: cannot move a non-`Copy` value out of a borrowed place`, and a keeping callee with a bare `x: D` parameter fails at the callee (`cannot give away parameter `x``). `consume(w.r)` with a bare parameter borrows: it prints `c1 end dD1`, one Drop. Pin: corpus/core/err_move_out_of_ref_to_keeping_callee (a field passed to a storing method), a:refused on mir-interp and mir-llvm.

title: `for g in v.into_iter()` DOES NOT CONSUME `v` OR MOVE ITS ELEMENTS, ON ALL FOUR SURFACES -- the element's `Drop` body runs after the loop instead of at the end of each iteration, TWICE when the loop moves `g` on (`let h = g`, `w.push(g)`), BEFORE the loop body reads the element when the iterator is bound first (`let it = v.into_iter(); for g in it`), and `v.len()` after the loop still compiles and prints 2, where design.md says `into_iter()` consumes the collection (v2 gives the spec's answer in every cell; the detail's cells 6-7, a loop over a temporary, owe no per-iteration drop: core-semantics §4.6 borrows a non-Iterator and §7.4 drops it at loop exit)
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: found while scoping B-2026-09-27-69, whose copy warning deliberately does not steer to `.into_iter()` because of this row. Measured 2026-09-27 on 1d152cc9e on `--interp`, JIT, `-O2` seq and `-O2` par, all four agreeing in every cell, valgrind 0 errors at -O0. Prefix: `struct D { id: i64, name: String }` with `impl Drop for D` printing `dD{id}{name}`, `fn mkd(n: i64) -> D` (name `n{n}`), `let v = vec![mkd(1), mkd(2)];`. design.md § Iteration: "`into_iter()` consumes it -- the caller cannot use the collection afterward", and § `for` loops: "To consume a collection while iterating, call `.into_iter()` explicitly (returns an owning iterator)". CELLS (got / owed): (1) `for g in v.into_iter() { println(f"g{g.id}"); } println("end")` prints `g1 g2 dD1n1 dD2n2 end`, owes `g1 dD1n1 g2 dD2n2 end` (each owned element dies at the end of its iteration). (2) `for g in v.into_iter() { let h = g; println(f"h{h.id}"); }` prints `h1 dD1n1 h2 dD2n2 dD1n1 dD2n2 end`, owes `h1 dD1n1 h2 dD2n2 end`: `h` runs each body and the iterator runs them all again. (3) `let mut w: Vec[D] = Vec.new(); for g in v.into_iter() { w.push(g); } println(f"l{w.len()}")` prints `dD1n1 dD2n2 l2 dD1n1 dD2n2 end`, owes `l2 end dD1n1 dD2n2`: the iterator runs the bodies of elements `w` now owns. (4) `let it = v.into_iter(); for g in it { println(f"g{g.id}"); }` prints `dD1n1 dD2n2 g1 g2 end`: both bodies run BEFORE the loop reads either element, so the loop reads values already destroyed. (5) `for g in v.into_iter() { println(f"g{g.id}"); } println(f"len{v.len()}")` compiles and prints `len2` after the bodies ran; it owes a use-after-move error. A bare `for g in v` is the other spelling and is correct by design: it borrows `v`, and moving `g` out is the documented copy, now reported by W0299 (B-2026-09-27-69). The loop over a TEMPORARY, which already owns its elements and is where a consuming `.into_iter()` over a local would naturally route, is wrong the other way (same four surfaces, same agreement, with `fn mkv() -> Vec[D] { vec![mkd(1), mkd(2)] }`): (6) `for g in mkv() { println(f"g{g.id}"); } println("end")` prints `g1 g2 end` and never runs either body, owes `g1 dD1n1 g2 dD2n2 end`; (7) `for g in mkv() { if g.id == 1 { break; } }` prints `end`, owes `dD1n1 dD2n2 end`. Moving the element on is right there (`let h = g` prints `h1 dD1n1 h2 dD2n2 end`), so the owning loop drops what it moves and loses what it keeps. The faults split four ways (the fourth is cells 6-7): the ownership checker does not mark `v` moved by `.into_iter()` (cell 5); the loop does not treat the element as owned, so nothing drops it per iteration and moving it on does not disarm the iterator's drop (cells 1-3); and a bound iterator drops its elements early (cell 4).

WIDENED 2026-09-30 by B-2026-09-29-107's fix (1b4b37092): a `Vec[D]` DESTRUCTURED out of the element is the same fault one level down. `for pair in v.into_iter() { let (a, j) = pair; let b = a; println(f"{j} {b.len()}") }` over `Vec[(Vec[D], i64)]` crashed on every compiled surface before that fix (valgrind 10); it is now memory-clean and prints `1 1 dD1 2 1 dD2 dD1 dD2 x` compiled against `--interp`'s `1 1 dD1 2 1 dD2 x` -- the leaf is a loop borrow, so `b` runs a copy's bodies and the collection runs them again, which is cell (2) here. The pattern spelling `for (a, j) in v.into_iter() { let b = a; .. }` and `out.push(a)` measure the same way. Unlike cells (1)-(3), `--interp` is right for these (it runs each body once, per iteration), so they are a run-vs-build split rather than an agreed fault.

UPDATE 2026-09-30, B-2026-09-29-109's fix: `--interp` now agrees with compiled on the DESTRUCTURE cells of the WIDENED note above. The interpreter treats an `.into_iter()` loop as lending its elements, as every compiled surface does, so a destructured leaf is a view there too. `for pair in v.into_iter() { let (a, j) = pair; let b = a; .. }` now prints `1 1 dD1 2 1 dD2 dD1 dD2 x` on all four surfaces, where the note recorded `--interp` as the right one. The destructure-only cell, `for pair in v.into_iter() { let (a, j) = pair; .. }` over `Vec[(D, i64)]`, used to run each body twice on `--interp` alone; it now prints one body per element at the loop's end, the same as compiled. Both are this row's fault (`into_iter()` consumes nowhere), and a fix here changes the two backends together.
fix: d3473e873d pins it; no code change was needed. The v2 pipeline (MIR builder, drop elaboration and the move checker; the legacy pipeline this row was measured on was deleted at M3, b910015b4d) gives the spec's answer in every cell, re-measured 2026-10-27 on main 0a4cfd7fc7 on mir-interp, mir-llvm, mir-llvm-asan and mir-build: (1) `g1 dD1n1 g2 dD2n2 end`; (2) `h1 dD1n1 h2 dD2n2 end`; (3) `l2 end dD1n1 dD2n2`; (4) `g1 dD1n1 g2 dD2n2 end`, the bound iterator no longer drops early; (5) refused by `karac check` as E0500 (value 'v' moved here, used again here). Cells (6) and (7), the loop over a temporary `mkv()`, print `g1 g2 dD1n1 dD2n2 end` and `dD1n1 dD2n2 end`: core-semantics §4.6 makes `for x in e` over a non-Iterator BORROW `e`, and §7.4 drops a `for` iterator temporary at loop exit, so the row's per-iteration expectation for those two cells is superseded by the spec, not owed. The WIDENED destructure cells print one body per element in its iteration (`1 1 dD1 2 1 dD2 x`), and `out.push(a)` keeps the parts until `out` drops. Pinned by corpus/core/for_into_iter_consumes (every cell, expected_from spec) and corpus/core/err_use_after_into_iter (E0500).

title: THE `borrow_projection_copy` LINT (W0299) IS STILL SILENT WHEN A BORROWED VALUE IS HANDED TO A KEEPING FREE-FUNCTION CALLEE -- `for g in v { let o = f(g); }` and `fn k(s: ref S) { let o = f(s.r); }` over `fn f(x: D) -> D { x }` copy the value and run its `Drop` body twice with no warning, where `let h = g` and `let o = s.r` now warn
detail: SOURCE NOTE: remainder of B-2026-09-27-69, whose fix (1d152cc9e) extends W0299 to a bare `for` element but keeps the lint's documented exemption for free-function arguments. That exemption was written for a DISCARDING callee: design.md § borrow_projection_copy measured `eat(s.r)` minting no copy and running the body once, which is still true (`for g in v { eat(g) }` prints each body once). A KEEPING callee is the case the exemption gets wrong. Measured 2026-09-27 on 1d152cc9e on `--interp`, JIT, `-O2` seq and `-O2` par, all four agreeing, valgrind 0: with `struct D { id: i64, name: String }` and `impl Drop for D` printing `dD{id}{name}`, `let v = vec![mkd(1), mkd(2)]; for g in v { let o = f(g); println("o"); } println("end")` prints `dD1n1 o dD2n2 o dD1n1 dD2n2 end` and `karac check` reports nothing. With `struct D { id: i64 }`, `struct S { r: D }` and `fn k(s: ref S) { let o = f(s.r); println(f"o{o.id}"); }`, `k(s)` prints `o1 dD1 dD1 end`, also with no diagnostic. Both runs match design.md's copy semantics, so the only gap is the warning. Telling the two cases apart needs the callee's keep/discard answer (does it return or store the parameter?), which the typechecker does not have today; ownership's `fn_moves_param_into_outliving_place` / `fn_conditionally_returns_param_bare` family answers it for codegen.
fix: 52ee6bb0ae and 31e471d60d (the v2 core's move rules as errors, C3, and moving out of a bare `for` element is an error), pinned by 0206d8dcd1. The row wanted W0299 to warn where a borrowed value went to a keeping free-function callee, because legacy copied it and ran its Drop body twice. Under core-semantics §3.7 that move is an error. Re-measured on the v2 pipeline at 1857b7091b: `for g in v { let o = f(g); }` over `fn f(x: own D) -> D { x }` fails with `cannot move 'g': it borrows its value (a bare `for` element ...). For a `for` element, iterate with `.into_iter()``; `fn k(s: ref S) { let o = f(s.r); }` fails with `cannot move a non-`Copy` value out of a borrowed place`; and the row's own `fn f(x: D) -> D { x }` (a bare parameter, which borrows under D5) fails at the callee with `cannot give away parameter `x``. Pin: corpus/core/err_move_for_element_to_keeping_callee, a:refused on mir-interp and mir-llvm.

2209d30ceb (pattern bindings follow the v2 core's modes, C3), pinned by 8163f29eae. Under core-semantics §3.7 moving a non-`Copy` part out of a value whose type has a `Drop` body is an error, and v2 applies it to the payload wherever it then goes. Re-measured at dcd242dbc8 with the row's three functions over `e: own E`: f1 (`E.A(r) => { return Some(r); }`), f2 (`let x = Some(r); return x;`) and f3 (`return r;`) each fail with `cannot move 'r' out of 'E', which has a `Drop` body (core-semantics.md §3.7): bind it as `ref r` to borrow it, or `.clone()` it inside the arm`, so the prelude-constructor shape no longer slips through and no backend runs. With the row's bare `e: E` (a borrow under D5) all three are refused too (`expected 'R', found 'ref R'` for f1/f2, `cannot give away `r`` for f3). Pin: corpus/core/err_enum_payload_drop_type_into_constructor (a:refused on mir-interp and mir-llvm), listed with the rules checked before MIR in borrowck's pin sweep (01b346f7d4).
title: `partial_move_of_drop_enum` MISSES A PAYLOAD MOVED INTO A PRELUDE CONSTRUCTOR -- `match e { E.A(r) => { return Some(r); } ... }` and `let x = Some(r); return x;` over an `enum E` with its own `impl Drop` compile without the error that `E.A(r) => { return r; }` gets, and the backends then disagree about the enum's body: `--interp` prints no `dE` and jit / `-O0` / `-O2` print it once per call. The lint asks `binding_only_borrowed_with`, which reads the bare `Some(..)` callee as an entry-copying free function, so `r` looks borrowed.
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: the same misreading B-2026-09-17-24's fix (9a60158b3) corrected in
`result_escape` for the codegen escape questions: a capitalized bare callee
(`Some`, `Ok`, `Err`) is a constructor, and its arguments are TRANSFERS. That
fix deliberately left the other `consume_class` callers unchanged, and this
lint (src/typechecker/items.rs, the `partial_move_of_drop_enum` emission) is
one of them.

    struct R { name: String }
    enum E { A(R), B }
    impl Drop for E { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("dE") } }
    fn f1(e: E) -> Option[R] { match e { E.A(r) => { return Some(r); } E.B => { return None; } } }
    fn f2(e: E) -> Option[R] { match e { E.A(r) => { let x = Some(r); return x; } E.B => { return None; } } }
    fn f3(e: E) -> R { match e { E.A(r) => { return r; } E.B => { return R { name: f"z" }; } } }

        karac check : error[partial_move_of_drop_enum] on f3's pattern ONLY

    with f3 removed and main printing both results' names:

        karac run --interp  :  a b
        karac run (JIT)     :  dE dE a b
        karac build -O0/-O2 :  dE dE a b
        valgrind -O0        :  12 allocs / 12 frees, clean

design.md § Part 8 `Drop` rejects moving a payload out of an enum with its own
`impl Drop`; f1 and f2 are that move, so both should be the same error f3
gets. Unflagged, the two backends pick different answers for whether `E`'s
body runs over the moved-from value.

Measured 2026-09-28 at 1e1a6c9 plus B-2026-09-17-26's fix, which does not touch
the typechecker.

title: A growth-heavy `Map[i64, i64]` workload runs 1.63x Rust's `HashMap` at equal hashing (SipHash-1-3 both), and ties a plain C linear-probing table: kata:325's bench, 857.5 ms against 520.6 for rust_ovf
detail: MEASURED 2026-10-02 on the 4-core x86-64 container, karac 0.1.0-dev.10181+gf2907d370, kata:325 `bench/max_sub_len.kara` (kara-katas `leetcode/301-400/325-maximum-size-subarray-sum-equals-k`). Workload: 60 scans of a 200,000-value array, each scan building a FRESH `Map[i64, i64]` of prefix sums with `get` plus `entry(p).or_insert(i)`; the three arrays give a few hundred, tens of thousands, and ~200,000 distinct keys, so most of the time goes to maps that grow 16 -> 262144 buckets on every call. bench.sh, 30 runs: kara 857.5 ms ± 23.6; rust -O 524.2; rust_ovf 520.6; go 662.0; c clang -O3 802.2 (a hand-written linear-probing table, 75% load, doubling, SipHash-1-3 over the key, i.e. kara's runtime design minus the control-byte tag); python 2110. All sinks `343512294`. So the gap is to hashbrown's design, not to the compiler's code around the map: the C table of kara's shape is within 7%. CALLGRIND (kara, 6.64 G Ir; rust 4.04 G; c 3.42 G): `karac_hash_word` 3.06 G self over 32,862,060 calls = 93 Ir a hash, 46% of the program; erased resize 1.29 G over 660 resizes (rust's `reserve_rehash` 0.64 G); mono `karac_map_i64_i64_get` 154 Ir a call inclusive; the erased `karac_map_entry` path 259 Ir a call inclusive (12,000,000 calls). System time is 2x rust's (120.7 vs 63.7 ms), consistent with the per-call tables being freshly faulted in. WHAT WAS TRIED: a mono `karac_map_<K>_<V>_entry` (insert_old's inline byte-walk probe minus the value store, wired at entry_chains.rs's claim) cut the per-call instruction path but ran SLOWER, 898.2 ms against 850.1 in the same hyperfine session, which fits B-2026-09-09-12's finding that the byte walk loses to the runtime's SWAR group scan on mispredicts. Not shipped; the patch is kept at kata-patches/mono_entry_proto.patch in the project folder. OPEN QUESTION for whoever owns Map performance: is 1.63x on a growth-heavy workload expected next to B-2026-09-07-53's projected 1.27x on kata:146 (a steady-size map), or a regression? The two biggest levers measured here are the hash (93 Ir, not inlinable because the hasher is a construction-time choice, B-2026-08-22-27) and resize. UPDATE 2026-10-27 (drop schedule, db4018cfb6): the word hash now runs from the module's own copy of SipHash-1-3, at 79 instructions a call, down from 93 (kata 340 measured; see B-2026-10-24-6). Kata 325 was not re-measured under callgrind: its wall time is inside noise (0.79-0.94 s against 0.87-0.93 s).

fix: 83cbad997f. The title's premise is legacy's: on v2, `for tok in s.split(",")` already walks a lazy StrSplit whose items are views, so no token allocates. The v2 cost was two runtime calls per token. The step found the separator through karac_mir_str_find, which built a StrSearcher per call (22% of the profile), and cut the piece through karac_mir_str_view, which ran its bytes through String::from_utf8_lossy (26%). Now a one-byte separator is scanned for in line (a one-byte needle is ASCII, so a matching byte never sits inside a char), and `slice` cuts a view in line whenever its clamped ends fall on char boundaries. A longer separator, or a cut inside a char, still goes to the runtime. Kata 331: 12.76G to 3.47G instructions and 0.96-1.07 s to 0.42-0.44 s, against legacy's 1.92 s and the row's Rust 434 ms. Guard test: tests/mir_build.rs mir_split_and_slice_cut_in_line (multi-byte separators, wide chars, slices out of range and inside a char; interpreter against -O0 and -O2), plus the same program on wasm32-wasip1.
title: (LEGACY PREMISE: on v2 the tokens were already views; the cost was two runtime calls a token, a StrSearcher build and a lossy re-borrow) `for tok in s.split(",")` heap-allocates and frees every token even when the loop only compares it, so kata 331's benchmark runs 5.3x Rust, 8.8x C and slower than CPython (2.31 s against 1.91 s)
detail: SOURCE NOTE: found benchmarking kata 331 (Verify Preorder Serialization), whose ★ arm is `for tok in preorder.split(",") { if slots == 0 { return false; } if tok == "#" { .. } else { .. } }` over strings of about 200,000 tokens. Measured on an x86-64 container, 30 runs each, karac built from main at bc22c5fe2 plus this thread's batch: Kāra 2.314 s, Rust `-O` 434 ms (`split(',')` iterates borrowed `&str`), C 262 ms (scans in place), Go 576 ms (`strings.Split` makes a slice of string headers that share the input's bytes), CPython 1.909 s. The sink matches in all five. callgrind on the Kāra binary: `karac_runtime_string_split` allocates each piece with its own `malloc(len)` + copy (runtime/src/lib.rs), and each element is freed through `karac_free_buf` when the temporary Vec drops, about 220 and 130 instructions per token respectively, out of about 520 per token in all (malloc, _int_malloc, malloc_consolidate, _int_free and free are over half the profile). Allocation count confirms it: one `malloc` per token plus the result buffer, and none for the iteration itself. The runtime already has a NON-OWNING String header (`{ptr, len, cap: 0}`, which the element drop skips; split uses it for empty pieces), so a split whose result cannot outlive its source could hand out views into the source. In `for t in s.split(sep)` the result is a temporary that dies with the loop while `s` lives on; what has to be proved is that `t` does not escape the body (no push, no store, no return, no move into a call that keeps it). Separately and cheaply, the scan compares a slice per byte position (`&hay[i..i+n] == needle`), where a one-byte separator could use `memchr`.

fix: 9abd7da4c8, on v2 (the row's legacy measurements predate M3). Before, every hashed-table lookup called karac_mir_map_find_hv: the probe ran through the key's `eq` glue, then the entry's index was counted through the Fenwick tree a holed table keeps, and karac_mir_map_at turned the index back into a pointer. That cost 62 instructions a lookup on kata 340, and `len()` was a call too. Now `MirMap` is `#[repr(C)]` with a six-word header (buf, entry_size, slots, holes, cells, ncells), and integer, `char` and `bool` keys are probed in line over the index. Every lookup hands back the entry pointer, so nothing counts an index: other keys use karac_mir_map_lookup_hv (or _lookup for a sorted table), and remove names the entry (karac_mir_map_remove_entry), which also drops the row's second hash on `remove`. `len()` and the walk of a hole-free table read the header in line. Kata 340: 5.59G to 3.93G instructions and 0.57-0.61 s to 0.39-0.49 s, against legacy's 3.61G and 0.39-0.46 s. Rust is not re-measured, since the Rust comparison is deferred until after M4. The remainder against Rust (the 93-instruction word hash, and karac_mir_map_remove_entry at about 200 instructions a call from Fenwick upkeep) is B-2026-10-24-6. Guard test: tests/mir_build.rs mir_table_lookups_agree_through_holes (holes, compaction, walks after removals, entry, get_or, indexing, set algebra, String keys, a sorted map; interpreter against -O0 and -O2), plus the same program on wasm32-wasip1.
title: AFTER B-2026-10-04-56 KATA 340'S `Map[char, i64]` BENCH STILL RUNS 1.85x RUST AT EQUAL HASHING (399 ms vs 216): each hash costs 92 instructions against Rust's ~74, the erased `remove` path hashes a key the `get` before it already hashed, and the mono insert costs ~70 instructions a call beyond its hash
detail: MEASURED 2026-10-04 on the x86-64 container, after the call-site hash landed: kara 3.43 G instructions (karac_hash_int 1.49 G over 16.2M calls, 92 Ir a call; main 0.79 G; karac_map_i32_i64_insert_old 0.70 G over ~10M calls; the erased remove path's KaracMap::lookup 0.26 G plus karac_map_remove_old 0.13 G), against rust -O's 1.98 G in all. THREE LEVERS, none tried yet. (1) The per-hash cost: karac_hash_int saves two registers and calls a cold init path from its entry (`push r14; push rbx` before the INIT check), and carries the nbytes clamp and branch; Rust inlines SipHash-1-3 into the probe. (2) `Map.remove` goes through the erased `karac_map_remove_old`, which hashes through the stored fn again, so the shrink step's `get(d)` then `remove(d)` is still two hashes; a mono remove taking the call-site hash would share it the way get and insert now do. (3) The mono insert body walks control bytes one at a time; B-2026-09-09-12's group scan only serves i64-key gets. SOURCE NOTE: the remainder of B-2026-10-04-56, split out when that row closed.

fix: 2c6b4da665 pins it; no code change in that commit. Re-measured 2026-10-27 on main 0a4cfd7fc7: the row's program passes `karac check` and prints `2` on mir-interp, mir-llvm and mir-llvm-asan, and so do both variations it records as refused (`let a = v[0].0; let n = v[0].1;` and `let pair = v[0]; let a = pair.0; let n = pair.1;`). The MIR borrow checker now gives the copied `ref Node` the node's origin, as core-semantics §1.1 and §5.3 require; the commit that changed it was not identified. Pinned by corpus/core/ok_ref_copied_from_a_tuple_element (destructured, by field and whole tuple, with `pop` and `clear`; passes on mir-interp, mir-llvm, mir-llvm-asan and mir-build). The kata entries that cited this row (589 preorder_frames and differential) now pass on mir-interp and mir-llvm. fix: bc3451e2bc. `f"{n}"` of a single integer no longer calls a runtime native. The compiled backend emits Shim::StringOfInt (src/backend/mir/callable.rs; body build_string_of_int in src/backend/mir/call.rs): count the digits, malloc that many bytes plus one for a sign, write them from the end, store the String. LLVM sees the malloc, so a string whose bytes nothing reads costs no allocation (the row's guess about legacy, confirmed in effect), and every other use loses the call. runtime karac_mir_string_of_i64/u64 had no other caller and are removed. Measured with a release karac on a 4-core container, min of 5, against a control built from the same tree with the old call restored: the row's 44M `f"{i % 7}"` loop went from 705 ms to 5 ms; kata 504's bench went from 1.58-1.60 s to 1.54-1.58 s (output = legacy.out), inside the 1.51-1.62 s the row gives for legacy. Legacy was not re-measured (deleted at M3). Edge values (0, +-1, 9/10, i64::MIN/MAX, u64::MAX, the i8/u8/i32/u32 limits) agree on the build, the ASan lane, the wasm build and the interpreter, pinned by tests/mir_string_of_int.rs (added to CI's codegen-e2e job).
title: A one-integer f-string `f"{n}"` still runs about 3x legacy on the v2 compiled backend after B-2026-10-13-20's fix: 44M `f"{i % 7}"` take 0.86 s on `karac build --mir` against 0.28 to 0.31 s on legacy `karac build`, and kata 504's bench 1.97 to 2.25 s against 1.51 to 1.62 s
detail: Measured with a release karac at 5a4a35bb58 on a shared 4-core container, min of 5 runs. Program: B-2026-10-13-20's `fn main() { let mut total = 0; for i in 0..44000000 { let s = f"{i % 7}"; total += s.len(); } println(f"{total}"); }`. WHAT IS LEFT (read in the optimized IR, not profiled): per iteration one call to `karac_mir_string_of_i64(out, v)`, which mallocs the digits' block, then the String's drop frees it. No thread-local access is left on this path. How legacy gets to 0.3 s was not read; a guess is that its lowering is visible to LLVM, which can then drop an allocation whose only use is `len()`. A digit-count-then-inline-write lowering in codegen would make the same thing possible here. SOURCE NOTE: remainder of B-2026-10-13-20 (closed by fdb1d5fc22 + 5a4a35bb58).

title: A bare list literal used only to be walked or read, `for step in [1, 9] { .. }` or `let steps = [1, 9]; steps[0] + steps[1]`, heap-allocates a `Vec` every time it is evaluated under `karac build --mir`, where legacy `karac build` keeps it on the stack (B-2026-10-02-70's fix): 1,000,008 allocations against 9 for a million evaluations, so kata 752's bench, which walks `[1, 9]` four times per visited lock setting, is 2.5x legacy
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: kata 752 (Open the Lock), its bench: kara-katas leetcode/701-800/752-open-the-lock/bench/open_lock.kara. The ★ arm's breadth-first search turns each of the four wheels both ways with `for step in [1, 9] { let next = at + ((digit + step) % 10 - digit) * place; .. }`, so the literal is evaluated four times per setting popped, some 14.5 million times over 3000 locks. Measured with a debug karac (`--features llvm`) and runtime archives built at kara 1a5c083e3a; the three src/ commits on main since (c287c03cec, e08f9131e9, 56a4cad109) do not touch literal or `for` lowering. Shared 4-core container, three runs each.

TIMES: `karac build --mir` as written 1.44 to 1.66 s; the same program with the literal written `Array[1, 9]` 0.80 to 0.85 s; frozen legacy `karac build` 0.58 to 0.67 s; C 0.40 to 0.46 s. So the natural spelling is 2.5x legacy and the `Array` spelling 1.3x.

ALLOCATIONS (valgrind): a micro program, a million iterations of `for step in [1, 9] { total += (i + step) % 7; }`: v2 1,000,008 allocs, 16,001,196 bytes (16 bytes each); legacy 9 allocs. The read-only `let steps = [1, 9]; total += (i + steps[0]) % 7 + (i + steps[1]) % 7;` is the same on v2 (1,000,008) and 9 on legacy. `for step in Array[1, 9]` on v2: 8 allocs. The bench: v2 as written 58 million `karac_mir_vec_alloc` calls from `karac.main` (callgrind: 19.7G instructions in all, of which malloc 2.6G, `_int_free` 3.1G, free 1.6G, `karac_mir_vec_alloc` 1.28G, `karac_realloc_or_panic` 1.2G) against legacy's 4.8G; with `Array[1, 9]`, 122,601 allocs in all.

READ: design.md § List literals makes `[a, b, c]` a `Vec` unless the expected type says otherwise, so the allocation is the literal semantics and eliding it is an optimisation, not a fix to typing. Legacy elides it in `compile_for` (`try_compile_for_scalar_vec_literal`, B-2026-10-02-70): a non-empty `Vec` literal of scalars or scalar tuples used as the `for` iterable becomes an entry-block `[N x T]` alloca. v2 lowers the literal through `prefix_literal` / `array_literal` in src/mir/lower.rs (around lines 5109 and 5151) and the `for` around line 5340, and nothing turns a literal that is never moved, mutated or grown into stack storage. The remedy is a hypothesis: the legacy rule at the `for` iterable, or more generally a MIR pass that demotes a `Vec` local built from a literal and only read (indexed, `len`, iterated) to a fixed array.

RELATED: B-2026-10-02-70 (the legacy twin, fixed), B-2026-10-15-56 (the out-of-line `vec_alloc` cost; this row is about the number of allocations, which that does not cover), B-2026-10-18-51 (the pre-size pass and `for`).

OWNER: the MIR builder (src/mir/lower.rs) or, for a demotion pass, the shared drop schedule. The kata keeps its natural `[1, 9]` and cites this row.

ALSO kata 755 (Pour Water, kara-katas ee8b4ac): its bench pours 2,000 drops on each of 6,000 landscapes and each drop walks `for d in [-1, 1]`. `karac build --mir` makes 12,042,010 allocations against 42,010 with `Array[-1, 1]` (valgrind), and runs 0.47 to 0.71 s (interleaved median 0.59) against 0.44 to 0.51 s with `Array[-1, 1]` and 0.28 to 0.33 s (median 0.32) for legacy on a copy with `*x` written `x`, which legacy needs. So the natural spelling is about 1.8x legacy there and the `Array` spelling about 1.5x.

ALSO kata 864 (Shortest Path to Get All Keys): its bench runs a breadth-first search over (cell, keys held) states and walks `for (dr, dc) in [(-1, 0), (1, 0), (0, -1), (0, 1)]` for every state it takes off the queue. `karac build --mir` makes 31,891,103 `malloc` calls from `main` (callgrind) for that list, 64 bytes each, and runs 1.52 to 1.55 s against 1.26 to 1.32 s with `Array[...]` and 0.84 to 0.88 s for legacy `karac build` (five interleaved runs each). Instructions: 15.76 billion natural, 11.30 billion with `Array`, 7.59 billion legacy; the rest of the gap is most likely the out-of-line deque calls (B-2026-10-13-36), whose `memcpy` goes through the PLT (not traced further). The kata keeps the natural spelling.
fix: 2dfab26e09. `Vec.from_array` of a non-empty array of plain-data elements now borrows the array (capacity 0, so nothing frees it) when the Vec is only read: its local is only borrowed, and the array is a single-use temporary of the same block. Bodies that suspend or hold par regions are excluded, as is a destination that is the return place, because a top-level `let` becomes a static table whose initializer writes the return place, and a Vec borrowing that initializer's stack would dangle. Measured on kata 864: 32.0M allocations down to 140k, and 1.35-1.51 s down to 0.92-1.03 s (legacy 0.90-0.95). Katas 752 and 755 were already allocation-free and are unchanged. KARAC_MIR_BORROW_LITERALS=0 turns it off. Guard test: tests/mir_build.rs mir_read_only_list_literals_borrow_their_array, run against the interpreter at -O0 and -O2, including a coroutine and par case.

a10f2705e6. A list literal handed to a container's element slot follows the element type, as at a `let` annotation: `Vec.push`, `Vec.insert`, `VecDeque.push_back` / `push_front`, and `Set` / `SortedSet` `insert` check a non-empty `[..]`, `vec![..]` or prefix/repeat literal against a concrete element type (new infer_element_arg, src/typechecker/method_vec_mutation.rs), and a generic call checks one against a slot an earlier argument already solved to any concrete type, not only an `Array` (exprs.rs, extending B-2026-09-25-8). The row's `best.push([0, 1])` on a `Vec[Array[i64, 2]]` checks and prints `1`; `[3]` into a `Vec[Vec[u64]]` builds a `Vec[u64]`; `v.push([300])` on a `Vec[Vec[u8]]` is refused as out of range. Both backends agree (`karac run` and `karac build`). Kata 801's table arm can drop its `Array[i64, 2]` binding. Fixture tests/core_strict_check.rs a_list_literal_into_a_container_element_follows_the_element_type; control arm on 88e8372c1d's src: 0 passed; 4 failed, fix 4 passed.
title: A list literal passed to a method of a generic receiver does not take the parameter's type as its expected type: `best.push([0, 1])` on a `Vec[Array[i64, 2]]` is refused with "expected 'Array[i64, 2]', found 'Vec[i64]'", while the same literal passed to a free function taking `Array[i64, 2]` is accepted
detail: design.md § List literals: "`[a, b, c]` is a `Vec` by default and follows the expected type: with an `Array[T, N]` or `Set[T]` annotation it builds that type." A free-function argument follows that rule: `fn first(a: Array[i64, 2]) -> i64` called as `first([5, 6])` passes `karac check`. A method argument whose parameter type comes from the receiver's type argument does not: `let mut best: Vec[Array[i64, 2]] = Vec.new(); best.push([0, 1]);` fails `karac check` (and `karac run --interp`) with `error[typecheck]: expected 'Array[i64, 2]', found 'Vec[i64]'` at the literal. Binding it first, `let row: Array[i64, 2] = [0, 1]; best.push(row);`, passes. Whole reproducer: `fn main() { let mut best: Vec[Array[i64, 2]] = Vec.new(); best.push([0, 1]); println(f"{best[0][1]}"); }`. Kata 801's table arm (kara-katas leetcode/801-900/801-minimum-swaps-to-make-sequences-increasing/min_swap_table.kara) binds each row with an `Array[i64, 2]` annotation before pushing it, citing this row; drop the binding once this is fixed. SOURCE NOTE: found writing kata 801.

fix: d5df59923c: the MIR borrow checker refuses, by type, a view-typed value stored in a field of a `shared` value (core semantics §5.7, §5.8), before the by-loan analysis and so also in bodies that take no loan: an Assign into a place whose projection takes a Field of a Shared-typed prefix (`s.items`, `(*s).items` through a `ref` handle) whose value is or holds a view (ref, mut ref, Str, slice, or a tuple/array/collection/struct containing one), and a call that lends such a field by `mut ref` beside an argument of a view type the field's type contains (`s.items.push(r)`). A generic instance's message names it: "the instance put[ref String] stores a view (`ref String`) in `s.items`, a field of a `shared` value ... [E0509]". `karac check` renders it through mir_check_text; the old E0509 "the result borrows" arm now applies only to its own text. Pinned by corpus/core/err_generic_instance_view_into_shared (the review's 5.8-generic-view-instance pin) and tests/mir_view_into_shared.rs (inline push, push through a parameter, generic push and assign refused; a shared value of a view type storing nothing, and an owned copy, still run). Control at 39ab5b9dea: 0 passed; 1 failed, fixed 1 passed. mir-llvm corpus `--filter shared` (1768 matched) and `--filter sync`: no new failure, only the new pin flipping to pass; check sweep over corpus and katas and package compare unchanged.
title: §5.8's instance check is absent: a generic instance whose body stores a view-typed value where a view may not go (pin 5.8-generic-view-instance, `put[ref String]` into a `shared` field) is accepted by `karac check`, `karac build --mir` and both MIR runs. (Narrowed 2026-10-22: §5.7's four placement rules are now refused by check too, through its MIR borrow check, as well as both MIR backends.)
detail:
SOURCE NOTE: conformance sweep of docs/core-semantics.md at b03f2bc51f (2026-10-19), sweep key R08. OWNER (proposed): Thread A (check) + borrowck (shared drop schedule). PINS: review/conformance-sweep-2026-10-19/pins/5.7-view-into-shared-field, review/conformance-sweep-2026-10-19/pins/5.7-view-into-channel, review/conformance-sweep-2026-10-19/pins/5.7-view-into-escaping-closure, review/conformance-sweep-2026-10-19/pins/9.2-closure-view-into-shared, review/conformance-sweep-2026-10-19/pins/5.8-generic-view-instance. SPEC: §5.7: "A view may not be stored in, or flow into: a field of a `shared`, `sync` or `frozen` type; a global; a channel; an escaping closure (§9.3)"; §9.2; §5.8: "An instance whose body stores a view-typed value somewhere a view may not go is an error". OBSERVED (target/release/karac built at b03f2bc51f; `karac check --output=json`, `karac __mir-run`, `karac __mir-llvm-run`): All four §5.7 pins: check accepted with no diagnostics; mir-interp and mir-llvm run them (print `x` / `3`). 5.8: check accepts; MIR refuses only because `Slot[T]` does not lower (see the generic-shared-struct row). A probe where the shared field outlives the viewed local IS refused by check and MIR borrowck (E0516), so the origins are tracked; only the placement rule is missing. Whether that is a soundness hole elsewhere is not established here (inferred: the R09 shape is one). MIR HALF DONE (shared drop schedule, 5d88defb6b + c634b6b2ab): the MIR borrow checker refuses with E0509 a view stored in a `shared` field, a view captured by a closure stored in a struct or `shared` field or pushed into a `Vec[Fn]`, and a view sent through `Sender.send` / `BoundedChannel.send`. All four §5.7 pins are refused on both MIR backends (tests/mir_escaping_view.rs). Two parts remain open: the `karac check` half (Thread A), and §5.8's instance check, which MIR still cannot reach because `Slot[T]` does not lower.

NARROWED 2026-10-22 (review thread's conformance resweep on main 502e55cb69; re-measured by Thread A on 1f454480f7 + local work): the four §5.7 pins are refused by `karac check` as well as both MIR backends, because check now runs the MIR move and borrow checks (9ee80c0104). `Slot[T]` now lowers, so 5.8-generic-view-instance reaches MIR, and it is accepted everywhere: `karac check` says `All checks passed.` and `__mir-run` prints `1`, where the pin expects `error: instance put[ref String] stores a view in a shared field (§5.8)`. Only the §5.8 instance check remains.

fix: dc28b584ce (with 34ef1e191e): `IntoIterator` is design.md's trait, `type Item; fn into_iter(own self) -> impl Iterator[Item = Self.Item]` (runtime/stdlib/into_iterator.kara), and Vec, VecDeque, Set, SortedSet, Map, SortedMap and Receiver implement it (their `into_iter` moved from the inherent impls). The three measured failures: (1) the spec-shaped impl is accepted and its `into_iter` runs; (2) `c.into_iter()` under `C: IntoIterator[Item = i64]` types as `impl Iterator[Item = i64]` and runs: a trait method's `-> impl Trait` lowers to each impl's hidden associated type (`$into_iter`, registered in impl_trait_assoc_types; src/ty.rs, src/typechecker/exprs.rs), normalized at the instance like `C.Item`; (3) `v.extend(bag)` / `d.extend(bag)` from a type that is IntoIterator and no iterator calls the library's `vec_extend_into` / `deque_extend_into`. Underneath: a return-position `impl Trait` now carries the generic names in scope where it was declared (`Type::Existential.scope`), which substitution, instantiation and type-variable resolution reach, so a generic function's or generic impl's witness (`VecIntoIter[T]`) lowers at each use, and a generic witness is published; a `for` over an `impl Iterator` yields its Item (it bound the whole existential before). Per design.md, `for x in b` over a type that is only IntoIterator is refused with a fix that writes `.into_iter()`. Pinned by tests/mir_into_iterator.rs (4 tests, each program on the interpreter and `karac build`). Control at 6368689d53: 0 passed; 1 failed, fixed 1 passed. Corpus entries naming into_iter/IntoIterator/extend/Receiver/impl Iterator (343): mir-interp fail set identical to the base, mir-llvm identical to a base build at 6368689d53; check sweep and package compare unchanged. Remainders filed: B-2026-10-27-9 (an impl method's signature is not checked against its trait's), B-2026-10-27-10 (inherent and trait methods of one name share an instance name), B-2026-10-27-11 (Iterable does not exist).
title: `IntoIterator` is not the spec's trait: the prelude's (runtime/stdlib/into_iterator.kara, CR-202) has `type Item; type IntoIter;` and no `into_iter` method, where design.md § Iteration gives `type Item; fn into_iter(own self) -> impl Iterator[Item = Self.Item]`. A spec-shaped impl is refused, a `C: IntoIterator` bound cannot call `.into_iter()`, and `v.extend(x)` on a user `IntoIterator` type passes check but the MIR builder refuses it

fix: 643e98ab75. Core semantics §9.3: a closure escapes when "it, or a value containing it, is returned", and an escaping closure captures by move (§9.1). The builder passed a closure literal for a generic function parameter (`map`'s `f: own FnV`) as a local view whatever happened to the call's result, so in `(0..n).flat_map(|i| (i + 1..n).map(|j| i * 10 + j))` the inner closure borrowed `i`, which dies when the outer closure returns while the `IterMap` holding the closure lives on. Check relays the MIR borrow check here, so check refused it too. `src/mir/lower.rs` `note_returned_closures` now walks the value a fn or closure body returns: through block, `if` and `match` tails, `return`, tuple, array and struct literals, and calls whose result type can hold a function. `closure_for_param` makes the closures it finds there escape. A call whose result cannot hold a function (`.sum()`, `.collect()`) consumes its closures, which keep borrowing. All the row's shapes now pass check and print the expected output on `__mir-run` and `__mir-llvm-run`: the `Copy` parameter, the local `base`, kata 816's non-`Copy` `x: String`, and Thread A's `fn adder(i) -> impl Iterator` over a parameter or a local. fix: ed9152f8a5: at max_connections, acquire waits in its task for a loan to come back, up to its timeout, and only then fails with Timeout; with max_waiters callers already waiting it fails with Busy at once. Pool.acquire is a suspending native on both backends: __ready (runtime karac_mir_ready_pool in runtime/src/mir.rs; interpreter ready_pool in src/mir/interp.rs) is ready once the pool has an idle value, room for a new one, or is closed; otherwise the task joins the pool's waiter count and parks by the deadline (mir_task::ready_by), and the acquire after the wait reads what it came to (karac_mir_pool_full / pool_verdict). Outside a task nothing can give a value back, so a full pool's acquire waits its whole timeout, and is Busy at once when max_waiters is 0. Pinned by tests/mir_pool_wait.rs (control on c33af903fc: 0 passed, 3 failed; fix: 3 passed) on both backends. Remaining limitation, documented in docs/library/pool.md: an acquire called through a function value inside a task cannot suspend yet (M4 item 4) and blocks the thread for its timeout.
title: Connection pool `acquire` never waits and has no `Busy`: at capacity it returns `Timeout` at once whatever the timeout, and `max_waiters` limits nothing, where docs/library/pool.md specifies waiting up to the timeout for a value to come back and `PoolError.Busy` at once when `max_waiters` callers are already waiting
detail: SOURCE NOTE: ADR-3 phase 2, the connection pool's library page (docs/library/pool.md, Thread C); the review thread ruled the spec 2026-10-21 (fallible factory, Duration timeout, waiting with max_waiters, close, own-self builder, Busy). A pool that fails the instant it is full collapses under load. `Busy` is load shedding (a 503, the metric an operator alerts on); `Timeout` means a caller waited the whole timeout, which points at a slow backend or leaked loans, so the two must stay distinct (review ruling). Needs suspending tasks: owner the drop schedule (src/codegen/mir/, stackless coroutines), with Thread C on the native side (interpreter natives, runtime pool). Tag: M4a-services.

de3fb51f66. A view method whose receiver is a reference to a struct of only references and scalars, which copies no reference field out and calls only views, is classified `ReceiverPointeeValue` (`through_ref_fields` in src/mir/lower.rs). Its result borrows what those references' referents hold, which is the source text for `IterByRef[StrWords]` and the Vec for `IterByRef[VecIter]`. It does not borrow the iterator the adapter lends. Borrowck adds the variant: `transfer_call` follows the receiver's pointee loans, and the `view` body check accepts it. A lending iterator's `next` (`-> Option[ref i64]` into its own Vec) is not a view, so `IterByRef` over one still holds the iterator; this is the case the drop schedule asked to pin. `karac check` empties library bodies, so methods on all-reference library structs (`IterByRef`) keep their bodies there, and a body with no `return` never qualifies. Without that, check accepted the lending case vacuously, an unsoundness caught during development.

Measured on de3fb51f66's tree: the page example prints `2 2 / -v / -x / a / b` on check, `__mir-run`, `__mir-llvm-run` and `__mir-llvm-asan`. A Vec `it.by_ref()` then `it.collect()` prints `1 1`. title: A list literal whose FIRST element is a `ref T` of a `Copy` `T` is typed `Vec[ref T]` even where a `Vec[T]` is expected: `for p in v.iter() { let u: Vec[i64] = [p]; }` is refused with "expected 'Vec[i64]', found 'Vec[ref i64]'" by `karac check` and `karac __mir-run`, while `[1, p]`, `let a: Array[i64, 1] = [p]`, `w.push(p)`, `let x: i64 = p` and `S { x: p }` are all accepted
detail: core-semantics §5.10: "A `ref T` or `mut ref T` whose `T` is `Copy` is read as a `T` wherever a `T` is expected: an operator operand, an argument, a `let` with a `T` annotation, a field or element of a literal, a return value." Measured at a719a6d597 on a `Vec[i64]` walked with `for p in v.iter()`: refused are `let u: Vec[i64] = [p];` (7:27), `let a: Vec[i64] = [p, 1];`, and the assignment `st = [p];` to a `let mut st: Vec[i64]`, each with the same message from `karac check` and from `karac __mir-run` (exit 3, 'error[mir]: typecheck'). Accepted, and printing the right values under `__mir-run`: `[1, p]` (a literal first element fixes the element type at `i64` and `p` is then read as one), `let a: Array[i64, 1] = [p]` (so the Array path does take the expected type), `w.push(p)`, `let x: i64 = p`, a tuple `(p, x)` against `(i64, i64)`, a struct literal `S { x: p }`, and `return p` from a `-> i64` fn. So the Vec path seems to take its element type from the first element rather than from the expected `Vec[T]` (not traced). Legacy `karac run --interp` accepts all of them. Same family as B-2026-10-19-32 (a list literal not taking the expected type when it is a generic method's argument), a different site: there the literal is an argument, here it is a `let` initialiser or an assignment's right side. The kata's natural line is `let mut stack: Vec[i64] = [p];` in 851's quietest-first arm; it is written `[*p]` (the explicit read §5.10 allows) until this closes. SOURCE NOTE: found writing kata 851 (Loud and Rich).

fix: cbcd20a557 implements the review thread's ruling (551b7e6630, library/core-types.md § Printing): of two equally short decimals that both read back, with the value exactly halfway between them, the even last digit is shown, as Python's repr does. Both backends print through src/format_spec.rs display_f64 / display_f32 (the runtime compiles it through `#[path]`), so one change covers `__mir-run`, `__mir-llvm-run` and built binaries. even_tie takes the shortest digits, and when the last one is odd checks whether the value lies exactly on the midpoint with either neighbour. A bit-level bound (the value's decimal places against the midpoint's) turns nearly every value away before any text is read. A midpoint that reads back as the value is then confirmed against the exact 1100-place expansion. The row's value now prints -75455689800034.62. Checked against Python's repr on 14000 values (random dyadic fractions, ties at 2^-1..2^-70, subnormals, values past 2^53): no difference, where the old printer differed on 127. Cost, min of 15 runs over 1M values in release: within noise on ordinary floats, about 4% on a tie-heavy set. Pinned by corpus/fixtures/mir_library/float_display_ties_to_even (expected_from decision; Python's repr of the same values), which the pre-fix binary fails on its first two lines, and by cases added to format_spec's display_f64_follows_the_printing_rules unit test. No existing pin held the old rounding. The apps thread can drop mini_geographiclib's fmt() workaround.
title: Float Display breaks an exact tie between two equally short decimals away from zero, where Python's repr keeps the even last digit: -75455689800034.625 prints -75455689800034.63 on every v2 backend and in `--interp`, Python prints -75455689800034.62; library/core-types.md § Printing says only "the shortest digits that read back", so which of the two is unspecified
detail: SOURCE NOTE: found writing kara-katas apps/cli/mini_geographiclib (the real-world apps thread, 2026-10-23), where one polygon area out of 581 output lines differed in its last digit from the Python oracle while every intermediate matched bit for bit. Measured at 9e09409535: `println(f"{-76034228193651.2 + 578538393616.5771}")` prints -75455689800034.63 under __mir-run, __mir-llvm-run and run --interp; `f"{x:.30}"` shows the value is exactly -75455689800034.625, so .62 and .63 both read back and are equally near. Rust's `{}` gives .63 too (the rendering is Rust's shortest-digits algorithm, which rounds the last digit half up). Python gives .62; over .125/.375/.625/.875 at that magnitude Python prints .12/.38/.62/.88 (half to even) and Kara .13/.38/.63/.88. Ties happen only where the value has few fraction bits (large magnitudes; 142 of 5847 sampled floats with at most 12 fraction bits), and both backends agree, so this is not an A/B fault: it is a spec question plus Python parity, which the spec already cites for the exponent rule ("as Python's repr does"). Either pin half-to-even in core-types.md (and implement it) or say the tie is unspecified. The app emulates Python's choice in its own fmt() using the exact `{x:.60}` expansion, listed in its source header and README. Owner: the review thread (spec conformance) for the decision.

fix: a97412f163 (src/mir/rc_borrow.rs read_scrutinee_parts) fixes the borrowed-parameter shape, kata 951's. In a count-safe body with no `mut ref` parameter, a tuple `t = (move e_0, ..)` is rewritten when each part is a copy of what a `ref` parameter points at (`e = copy (*a)`, `e = retain(*a)`, or `r = &(*a); e = <native>.clone(move r)`) and `t` is only read part by part and dropped. Then `t.i..` reads `(*a_i)..`, and the copies and the tuple's drop go. A handle bound out of a part is then a retain of a borrowed parameter's handle, which the existing elision removes, so `eqv` in the guard has no clone, drop or release left. Measured on the kata 951 bench (release, `karac build`, same container): 1.30 s with KARAC_MIR_RC_BORROW=0, against 0.42-0.44 s with the pass, with identical output. The nested-match spelling measured 0.38-0.40 s. Guard: tests/mir_scrutinee_parts.rs runs the interpreter at -O0 and -O2. It covers a scalar part, String parts, a body that writes through a `shared` field (copies kept), and a match that binds the whole tuple (kept). It asserts no `clone.` / `drop.` / `last.` call in eqv's IR. The control arm with KARAC_MIR_RC_BORROW=0 fails at `0 passed; 1 failed`, and the ASan lane runs it clean. The original kata 558 shape is NOT covered: a tuple of retained handle LOCALS that outlive it needs proof that each source is neither moved nor dropped before the tuple's last read. It is split out as B-2026-10-24-11; the row measured its cost there as within noise.
title: (NOT SMALL, kata thread 2026-10-24: 3.4x on kata 951's tuple match of two Option[shared] params, 1.31 s vs 0.39 s for nested matches) A `match` on a tuple of handle locals (`match (top_left, top_right, bottom_left, bottom_right) { (Quad.Leaf(p), ..) => .. }`) counts each handle into a built tuple and releases the tuple after the match, although the arms only read discriminants and Copy payloads: kata 558's `intersect` pays four increments and four `drop.shared` calls per Split node for it, 8 of the 8 count sites its IR has left
detail: SOURCE NOTE: the remainder of B-2026-10-14-9, measured 2026-10-23 on main b854ea64ad. The elaborated MIR of kata 558's `intersect` (corpus/katas/501-600/558-*/bench/quad_tree_or) builds `_30 = (move _31, move _32, move _33, move _34)` from `_31 = retain(_17)` .. `_34 = retain(_26)`, matches `_30` by its fields' discriminants and `bool` payloads, and ends with `drop(_30)`. The four sources stay alive and are used afterwards (`Quad.Split(top_left, ..)`), so `rc_pairs` cannot cancel the pairs, and `rc_borrow` applies only to handles read out of `ref` parameters. In the IR (KARAC_MIR_LL) that is the 4 `add i64 .., 1` and 4 `drop.shared Quad` calls left in `kara.intersect` on the Split/Split path. core-semantics §6.1 says using a handle aggregate as a value counts its handles; whether a tuple built only to be matched is a use as a value is the open question. A lowering that matches each element place directly (no tuple), or a pass that leaves the tuple's fields uncounted when the tuple is only read and its sources outlive it, would remove the counts. Inferred cost: small. Removing the other 8 sites (570645fbea) moved the full bench from 1.99-2.10 s to 1.97-2.05 s, within noise; v2 already beats legacy on this bench (1.97-2.05 s vs 2.46-2.74 s). MEASURED 2026-10-24 by the kata thread at 086f304909 (release, karac build --mir): kata 951 (Flip Equivalent Binary Trees), whose natural arm is `match (root1, root2) { (None, None) => true, (Some(a), Some(b)) => .., _ => false }` over two bare (borrowed under D5) `Option[TreeNode]` params of a `shared struct`. Every call clones each parameter into the scrutinee tuple (`clone.Option[shared TreeNode]`) and drops the tuple at the end (`drop.(Option, Option)`), two increment/decrement pairs per call on handles only read. Bench (50,000 rounds x 20 pairs of 100-node trees): tuple match 1.31 s median, 9.55 G instructions; the same function as nested matches 0.38-0.40 s, 3.79 G, no clone or drop left, identical output; Rust Rc<RefCell> with overflow checks 0.52 s, 5.25 G; C 0.37 s, 3.99 G. So on this shape the tuple counts make v2 3.4x slower than the nested spelling and 2.5x Rust, contradicting the 'Inferred cost: small' above, which held only for kata 558.

fix: dd769270e7 (with a1ce2f4ed4): all four pieces on v2. (1) `%show <expr>` runs the expression as a cell would (from the values the cells left, under the open providers, without changing the session) and renders the value the snapshot writer records: src/repl/display.rs `render_source` reads the source form as a tree, shows numbers without suffixes, nested values one item to a line, a Map's or Set's elements in order (a Map walks in hash order), and a list of one struct type also as a text/html table (columns alphabetical, HTML-escaped, as the kernel's pins expect); a value with no source form (a function, a `shared` value, a handle) is refused saying so, and errors name `%show:L:C`. The kernel's two `%show` tests run again. (2) `--auto-clone` and `%set auto-clone on|off`: a cell refused only because it uses bindings an earlier cell moved away gets `.clone()` inserted where each moved (in cell history, so `:save` carries it, and in the replayed source), a `perf[auto-clone-in-repl]` note per clone, and runs again; the cells from the rewritten one on replay once, from the values that cell started from, so earlier cells do not run again. A move inside a provider scope's cell is not rewritten (its `let`s replay apart). (3) `:provide R = expr` runs `with_provider[R](expr, || {})`, so a provider without R's trait is refused when the scope opens. (4) The construction program, `%show` and cells under a provider start from the values; closing a scope keeps them. Also fixed on the way: a provider scope's `let`s replayed OUTSIDE the scope, so `let k = Clock.now();` under `:provide Clock = FakeClock {}` read the real clock in every later cell; they replay inside it now. And `:save` terminates each statement cell, so a cell ending without `;` no longer breaks the export. Pins flipped: `repl_v2_show_and_auto_clone_are_supported`, `repl_v2_auto_clone_flag_clones_a_moved_binding`; new: `repl_v2_provide_refuses_a_provider_without_the_trait`, `repl_v2_provide_does_not_run_an_earlier_cell_again`, `repl_v2_show_renders_values`, `repl_v2_show_prints_errors_and_providers`, `repl_v2_auto_clone_clones_where_the_binding_moved`, plus 7 display unit tests.
title: The v2 REPL's remaining legacy-only pieces: `%show` and `--auto-clone` / `%set auto-clone` refuse on v2, `:provide` does not check that the provider implements the resource's trait until the next cell, and the `:provide` construction program still replays every earlier cell
detail: SOURCE NOTE: split from B-2026-10-23-6 when its value snapshots landed (7e5765dd1b), which closed the replay of earlier cells for ordinary statement cells. What is left, measured at 7e5765dd1b: (1) `%show` renders the legacy interpreter's `Value` (src/repl/display.rs) and refuses on v2, naming `karac repl --legacy`; Debug formatting (`{x:?}`) is not implemented on v2, so v2 has no text form to fall back on (the snapshot writer `source_of` in src/mir/interp.rs gives a source form, which may serve). (2) Auto-clone rewrites the legacy checker's cross-cell use-after-move; on v2 the D5 rules make most of those moves borrows, and a moved binding is now left out of the next cell (a use of it is refused through the replay and names the moving cell). (3) `:provide Clock = FakeClock {}` opens the scope on v2 although `FakeClock` does not implement `ClockProvider`: the construction check runs the expression under the providers already open, not under the new one, so the error appears at the next cell. (4) The `:provide` construction program (src/repl.rs, the synth that ends in `crate::cli::repl_v2::run_cell(&synth)`) still replays `persistent_lets`, so opening a provider runs the earlier cells' side effects again; cells under an open provider replay too (their `let`s only), as before. title: A long `sort_by` of shuffled pairs on the MIR compiled backend runs 1.5x legacy and about 1.9x Rust after B-2026-10-13-18's partition: kata 252's bench is 0.28-0.30 s against legacy's 0.19 s, and 1,000,000 indices sorted by key 10 times take 0.93-1.05 s against rustc -O's 0.51-0.56 s
detail: SOURCE NOTE: the remainder of B-2026-10-13-18, measured 2026-10-24 at 6566f6fa2c with a release karac on a shared container. Shuffled input now partitions (the ord band in sort_order and the part_sort shim), with the cursors in registers and the buffers swapping each level. What legacy's unstructured arm still does that v2 does not (src/codegen/vec_method.rs emit_sort_partition_body, read, not measured on v2): an insertion-sorted leaf of 64 where v2 merges the leaf through merge_widths (legacy measured 353M -> 313M cycles for that change, B-2026-08-16-3), a fused scatter whose cursors converge from both ends, a count pass with a vectorize hint, and a randomly chosen pivot. A leaf change alters which comparisons the comparator sees, so the interpreter's partition must change with the shim (tests/mir_build.rs mir_unstructured_sort_partitions_on_both_backends checks they agree). Inferred, not measured: the leaf is the larger part, since about log2(64) of the log2(n) levels' work happens in the leaves. MEASURED 2026-10-27 at fc21ee1d4c (release karac, callgrind on a 4-round copy of the bench, 272M Ir): the partition shim is 73.5% (the count pass vectorizes to about 8 instructions per element; the scatter is about 20, through select chains over the three cursors), merge_widths 21%, main 5%. Two levers tried against a saved control binary, min of 5 runs twice, output matching legacy.out: an insertion-sorted leaf of 64 in both the interpreter and the shim, and a scatter that branches on the rare tied tag and selects between only the lt and gt cursors. Neither moved the bench outside noise (0.274-0.288 s against 0.278-0.281 s for the scatter), so both were reverted. Not yet tried: legacy's converging cursors (needs the gt run's order restored to stay stable) and a random pivot. The kata is under M2's 2x per-bench bar.

detail: Found by the M3 item 11 deletion. Decide per item whether the pin or v2 is right (the errdefer order is a semantics question for core-semantics, not a rendering one). Ignored tests (full list with reasons): review/m3-item11/ignored-v2-gaps.txt in the shared folder; each carries `#[ignore = "v2 gap after M3: ..."]`.
fix: 0bb0c20d38. Per item: (1) `main`'s `Err(e)` exit now writes `e` through its `Display` impl on `karac run`, `__mir-run`, `__mir-llvm-run` and a built binary: `lower_instance` queues the Display instances `main`'s return type contains (`queue_nested_displays`), which the backends' error exit already calls for a nested value. (2) A failed `requires` / `ensures` now panics with `contract violated: requires clause` / `ensures clause` at the clause (was `explicit panic` at 0:0), and `--output=json` carries it in `runtime_errors`; `--release` still strips it. (3) The errdefer order was the pin's error, not v2's: core-semantics §7.7 puts `errdefer` in the one LIFO with `defer`, which v2 already runs (`e2 d2 e1 d1`); the pin is flipped. title: MIR borrowck lets the borrowed place change while a ref read through a borrowed struct's `mut ref` field is still live, a use-after-free that `karac check` accepts
fix:
930b560ed5. `Origins::live_loans` in src/mir/borrowck.rs now closes the live set over held loans. A live loan of a place that is not reached through a deref keeps everything that place's local holds live, transitively. This is the 'a: 'b of a `&'b Lend<'a>`, applied at liveness time, so the origins dataflow is unchanged. A reborrow through `r` already holds `r`'s loans from `transfer`, so a deref place is skipped. Both callers, `borrow_errors` and `loan_liveness`, use it, so the borrow-flag liveness in flags.rs is extended the same way. The drop schedule reviewed the diff before the push and did not object.

Measured on 930b560ed5's tree. The row's program is refused at 13:5 E0516, by `karac check` (`cannot mutably borrow \`o.v\` while it is still borrowed`) and by `__mir-run`. With the `*x` read moved before the push, it is accepted and prints `1` then `4` on the interpreter and at -O0..-O3. A lending `Iterator` written the same way (`next -> Option[ref i64]` reading `self.o.v`) is now refused too. Control: de3fb51f66's tree (built in a scratch worktree) accepts the row's program and prints 1, and ASan reports `heap-use-after-free`.

Corpus mir-interp on the debug binary: none of the 47 failures that mention a borrow is new; all of them fail identically on de3fb51f66. The run covers the whole corpus in two passes, and the remainder (katas 920+, katas/apps, backend, bespoke, oracle, tools) has no borrow failures. Fixture: `mir_a_ref_read_through_a_borrowed_holder_keeps_its_loan` (tests/mir_build.rs). Gate: fmt, both clippy legs, `cargo test` 8867 passed / 0 failed, and `cargo test --features llvm` 9276 passed / 35 failed. All 35 failures were stale archives (a runtime change upstream); after rebuilding lean, unicode and full, the five binaries that held them pass: mir_build 211, mir_collections 39, mir_default_generic_shadow 2, mir_json 2, mir_map_hash 1.

title: After the in-line Map probe (9abd7da4c8), kata 340's sliding window still pays about 200 instructions per `remove` in karac_mir_map_remove_entry (Fenwick upkeep on a holed table, a rebuild on the first hole, and compactions) and 79 per word hash (93 before db4018cfb6), against Rust's ~74, so v2 sits at legacy's 3.6-3.9G instructions where Rust -O ran 1.98G
detail: SOURCE NOTE: the remainder of B-2026-10-04-79, measured 2026-10-24 at 9abd7da4c8 on the x86-64 container (callgrind, kata 340 bench longest_k_distinct): 3.93G instructions in all; karac.main 1.37G (in-line probes), karac_hash_word 1.23G over 13.2M calls (93 each), karac_mir_map_remove_entry 0.60G over 2.98M calls (200 each) plus its rebuild/compaction helpers 0.37G and 0.23G. Levers: (1) keep the Fenwick tree lazy, rebuilt only when an index is asked of a holed table (only walks ask since lookups hand back pointers), which needs care because concurrent readers share a table; (2) inline the word hash (SipHash-1-3 of one word) instead of calling karac_hash_word; (3) cheaper compaction thresholds for small tables. The Rust comparison is deferred until after M4 (Gowtham 10-13), so this is low. UPDATE 2026-10-27 (drop schedule, db4018cfb6): lever (2) done out of line. Each module defines karac.hash.word, SipHash-1-3 from a state the seed precomputes (karac_hash_word_state), called memory(none) as before. Fully in line it ran SLOWER (kata 340 0.45 -> 0.55-0.59 s, kata 219 1.25 -> 1.65 s), because the seed loads could not be shared across the stores between a get and an insert of one key. Kata 340 is now 3.81G instructions (from 4.02G), with the hash at 79 a call. Levers (1) and (3), the remove path, are untouched.
